findings.failure_path: The plan states that template confirmation 'already exists and is fully rolled out' without citing any evidence. That's an unsupported universal claim, and the rest of the plan depends on it.
findings.smallest_fix: Cite the rollout evidence (flag state, coverage of every export path), or soften the wording to the scope that has actually been verified.

findings.failure_path: The requester asked for the template to be checked and fixed automatically before export, with post-export differences only recorded for observation. The plan has no pre-export check. It renders first and checks afterwards. A failed or missing post-render check then blocks publishing to the shared folder and notifying subscribers. That makes the step the requester wanted as observe-only into a blocking gate, and the check the requester wanted before export never happens.
findings.smallest_fix: Move the check-and-fix step before rendering. Make the post-render comparison record-only: log the differences and do not block publish or notify. Drop the credential and the private holding area.

findings.failure_path: When a difference is found, the plan rewrites the template mapping, rules out automatic re-render, and waits for the user to reconfirm. The requester asked for an automatic fix, so this replaces it with a manual loop and the export stalls until the user responds. The export service also edits a shared template mapping in place. That can change other in-flight exports bound to the same template version, and the service ends up correcting the same template it is checked against.
findings.smallest_fix: Before export, apply the correction automatically to a new template version scoped to this export job, then render from it. Do not edit the shared mapping in place, and do not require user reconfirmation.

findings.failure_path: Manual downloads skip the check, so they deliver reports that were never checked or fixed. That contradicts the step-1 claim that the check cannot be skipped and leaves a route around the requested fix.
findings.smallest_fix: Run the same pre-export check-and-fix for manual downloads. Only the post-export difference report should arrive asynchronously.

findings.failure_path: The requester's words do not ask for a staged rollout by team and report family, an enforce mode, or an admin permission to bypass the gate. These add switches and permissions beyond the request, and the override weakens the check.
findings.smallest_fix: Drop the per-team and per-report-family enforcement stages and the admin bypass permission. If staging validation is still wanted, keep it as a plain rollout note.

findings.failure_path: Sampling pages cannot show that every field matches the template, so a per-field checklist built from a sample overstates what was checked. Separately, when the check is unavailable, reports stay in the holding area with no stated retry, timeout or release path, and nothing defines what the check does when the user chose 'none' as the template option.
findings.smallest_fix: State what is actually checked, either full coverage or explicitly sampled. Define retry and timeout behaviour when the check is unavailable. Define what happens for the 'none' option.

findings.failure_path: 'cannot skip the check' is an absolute claim. Manual downloads (line 10) and the admin override (line 12) both contradict it.
findings.smallest_fix: Remove the absolute wording, or remove the bypass paths so the claim holds.

findings.failure_path: The plan says template confirmation 'already exists and is fully rolled out' but cites no evidence. Step 1 also describes new binding of the choice to the template version, export job and data snapshot, so the existing feature may not cover what this plan relies on.
findings.smallest_fix: Cite evidence for the existing rollout, and list the step-1 binding as new work.

findings.failure_path: The plan names no tests or acceptance evidence. Nothing would fail if a template were left unfixed before export, if the post-export comparison blocked publishing, or if a bypass path skipped the check.
findings.smallest_fix: Add test cases that fail on each of these: a template mismatch left unfixed before export, a recorded post-export difference blocking publish, and manual downloads or the admin path skipping the check.

findings.failure_path: The requester asked for an automatic check and fix of the report template before export. In the plan, rendering 'runs as today' and the check only happens afterwards. Step 3 (line 8) then has the export service revise the mapping and wait for the user to reconfirm. Nothing is checked or fixed automatically before export, so a report built on a wrong template is still rendered, and fixing it depends on a person.
findings.smallest_fix: Move the check before rendering. When the template or its mapping differs from the confirmed template, fix it automatically, then render. Drop the 'wait for the user to reconfirm' step on the pre-export path.

findings.failure_path: The requester said differences found after export should only be recorded for observation. The plan instead blocks publishing to the shared folder and notifying subscribers on a post-render credential, and keeps unchecked reports in a private holding area. Exports that the request lets through are delayed or blocked, and any outage of the checker stops publishing.
findings.smallest_fix: Make the post-export check record-only: log each difference for observation and publish and notify as today. Drop the publish credential and the private holding area.

findings.failure_path: Manual downloads skip the check entirely and only get a report later. Downloaded reports never get the pre-export automatic fix, so they can differ from the confirmed template. Users can also reach the same content through a download that the shared-folder path blocks, which makes the gate inconsistent.
findings.smallest_fix: Run the same pre-export check and automatic fix for manual downloads. Keep only the after-export recording asynchronous.

findings.failure_path: The request does not need several of the controls in step 5. The per-team and per-report-family 'enforce the gate' rollout, the admin permission override and the step 1 binding that stops the export service from skipping by omitting the template (lines 2-4) all exist to enforce a post-export gate the requester never asked for. The admin override also creates a privileged path around the check that has no audit trail.
findings.smallest_fix: Drop the admin bypass permission and the enforcement rollout stages. Roll out the pre-export automatic fix with simple staging validation, and leave post-export differences in observe-only mode.

findings.failure_path: The plan never says how a template change made by the check is stored. If the automatic fix overwrites the confirmed template or mapping in place, it can silently destroy the user's confirmed layout, with no way to roll back or audit what changed.
findings.smallest_fix: Write each automatic fix as a new template or mapping version linked to the confirmed version. Record the diff, and allow a revert.

findings.failure_path: The plan contains no tests and names no evidence. Nothing would catch an automatic fix that produces a wrong mapping, the checker passing when it is unavailable, or a mismatch slipping through the page sampling. Because the checker only samples pages, a verified credential does not show that the whole report matches the template.
findings.smallest_fix: Add test cases: a mismatched template is fixed before export, an unavailable checker produces a fault and not a pass, and a mismatch on an unsampled page is either covered by the check or explicitly called out as unverified.

findings.failure_path: The Status line says template confirmation 'already exists and is fully rolled out', but the plan cites no evidence for it. Step 1 also describes binding the choice to the template version, export job and data snapshot, which may be new work presented as existing. If that binding does not exist yet, the plan's scope and rollout risk are understated.
findings.smallest_fix: Cite evidence for the existing confirmation feature, or reword the claim. State explicitly which parts of step 1 are new, such as binding the choice to the export job and data snapshot.

findings.failure_path: The requester asked for this: 「导出前自动检查并修正报表模板；导出后的差异只记录下来做观察」. The plan does something different. Its only check runs after rendering, and that check decides whether the report can be published or sent to subscribers. So nothing checks or fixes the template before export. Post-export differences, which were meant only to be recorded, now block delivery. The core intent is reversed in both places.
findings.smallest_fix: Move the automatic template check and fix to before rendering and export. Make the post-export comparison write a difference record for observation only. Remove the publish/notify gate, the credential and the private holding area.

findings.failure_path: When a difference is found, the export service changes the template mapping and then waits for the user to reconfirm. This happens after export. The request asked for an automatic fix before export and nothing beyond recording afterwards. A service rewriting shared template mappings from post-export results is also an unrequested mutation. It can silently change the template for other jobs and users. Waiting for reconfirmation leaves the report stuck, with no timeout.
findings.smallest_fix: Apply template fixes automatically in the pre-export step, scoped to the current export job, and keep the confirmed template version unchanged or versioned. After export, only log the differences. Remove the step where the service revises the mapping and waits for reconfirmation.

findings.failure_path: Manual downloads skip the check and get their report later. That means manual exports never get the requested pre-export check and fix. It also contradicts step 1's claim that the export service 'cannot skip the check'. Under the plan's own gate, unchecked content can leave through download while shared-folder publishing is blocked.
findings.smallest_fix: Run the same pre-export check and fix for every export path, including manual downloads. Treat only the post-export difference record as asynchronous.

findings.failure_path: Step 5 adds a staged enforcement rollout (one team and one report family at a time) and an admin permission that bypasses the gate. Step 2 adds a credential bound to the template and data snapshot. The request needs none of these. The admin bypass also contradicts the claim that the check cannot be skipped. All of this adds permission surface and upkeep cost.
findings.smallest_fix: Drop the admin bypass, the per-team and per-family enforcement rollout, and the credential binding. If staging observation is kept, add explicit exit and rollback criteria.

findings.failure_path: The check samples only some pages and then issues a credential that the report 'matches' the template. Pages that weren't sampled can still differ, so the credential claims more than the check covers. If the check service is down, every report stays in the holding area and subscribers are never notified. The plan has no timeout, retry or recovery path for this.
findings.smallest_fix: Do the pre-export check on the template and field mapping deterministically, so it covers the whole template. Label any post-export sampling as partial observation data. Say that a check outage produces a logged fault and does not block delivery.

findings.failure_path: The plan names no tests or evidence. Nothing would fail if the pre-export fix were skipped, if post-export differences blocked delivery, or if manual downloads went out unchecked. That leaves the acceptance criterion 'can be implemented and rolled out safely' with nothing to show it is met.
findings.smallest_fix: Add verification steps: a test that a template mismatch is fixed before export for every export path, including manual download. Add a test that a post-export difference produces only a record and never blocks or changes anything. Add a test of how a check outage is handled.

findings.failure_path: The plan states that template confirmation 'already exists and is fully rolled out', without citing any evidence. Step 1 says the export service 'cannot skip the check', but steps 4 and 5 describe ways to skip it. Both are absolute claims that nothing backs up.
findings.smallest_fix: Cite evidence for the rollout status (for example, coverage per export path) or soften the wording. Remove 'cannot skip' or make it true for all paths.

findings.failure_path: Rendering runs unchanged and checking begins afterward, so an incorrect template mapping reaches the exported artifact without the requested automatic pre-export correction. Manual downloads also receive only a later check report.
findings.smallest_fix: Add automatic template validation and correction before rendering for every export path, including manual downloads. Render from the corrected mapping.

findings.failure_path: A post-render difference or checker outage prevents publication and subscriber notification and leaves reports in holding. This contradicts the requirement that post-export differences only be recorded for observation.
findings.smallest_fix: Remove post-render release credentials, publication and notification gating, and private holding. Record observational differences and checker faults without blocking delivery.

findings.failure_path: An observational difference changes the template mapping and requires user reconfirmation. This introduces an unauthorized mutation and manual dependency, while the already-rendered artifact still uses the previous mapping.
findings.smallest_fix: Make post-export observation record-only. Perform automatic correction before export and remove the post-export mapping mutation and reconfirmation requirement.

findings.failure_path: The plan introduces keep/adapt/none decisions and an anti-omission enforcement contract beyond checking an already-confirmed template. These modes can change or remove the comparison target, and no evidence establishes that template-omission hardening addresses a risk introduced by this change.
findings.smallest_fix: Consume the existing confirmed template and version. Drop additional mode selection and split anti-omission hardening out of this change; document any existing choices as verified baseline behavior.

findings.failure_path: Per-team and per-report-family enforcement plus an admin bypass introduce rollout restrictions and a new permission for an unwanted post-render gate. They create different export semantics by cohort and role without support in the request.
findings.smallest_fix: Drop the post-render enforcement cohorts and admin bypass permission. Validate and roll out the requested pre-export correction with post-export observation remaining record-only.

findings.failure_path: Observing staging has no specified assertions or acceptance evidence, so the proposed reversed ordering, manual-download omission, and observational mutations could all survive rollout validation.
findings.smallest_fix: Specify acceptance cases proving automatic correction before export, including downloads, and proving that post-export differences or observation outages neither mutate templates nor block delivery.

findings.failure_path: The unconditional claim that template confirmation is fully rolled out has no cited implementation or deployment evidence. The plan depends on that claim to supply a confirmed template across export paths.
findings.smallest_fix: Cite evidence for confirmation behavior and rollout coverage, or mark this prerequisite unverified and require verification before implementation relies on it.

findings.failure_path: Rendering proceeds unchanged and validation happens afterwards. A wrong template mapping therefore reaches rendering, and manual downloads can deliver it before any correction. This omits the requested automatic pre-export check and repair.
findings.smallest_fix: Validate and automatically correct the template before rendering on every export path, including manual downloads; define the outcome when correction fails.

findings.failure_path: A post-render difference or checker outage prevents publication and subscriber notification and leaves the report in holding. This turns observation into a delivery dependency, contradicting the request that post-export differences only be recorded.
findings.smallest_fix: Remove the post-export publication credential, notification gate and private holding requirement. Record post-export differences and checker failures without blocking delivery.

findings.failure_path: A detected difference mutates the template mapping and requires user reconfirmation, while the existing artifact remains unchanged because there is no re-render. This violates observation-only handling and adds manual intervention instead of automatic pre-export correction.
findings.smallest_fix: Make post-export handling record observations only. Move automatic correction before rendering and remove the reconfirmation step.

findings.failure_path: The keep/adapt/none selector adds an unrequested manual decision and introduces modes that can abandon the confirmed template. The associated omission-prevention hardening expands the feature beyond checking and correcting that template.
findings.smallest_fix: Reuse the confirmed template and its version. Drop the new mode selection and confirmation ceremony, and split broader omission-prevention hardening into separately scoped work.

findings.failure_path: The team-by-team and report-family enforcement rollout introduces eligibility restrictions for an out-of-scope post-export gate. It does not establish delivery of the requested pre-export correction across export paths.
findings.smallest_fix: Drop the cohort enforcement requirement. Retain staging validation focused on automatic pre-export correction and observation-only post-export handling.

findings.failure_path: The admin override adds an unrequested permission and bypass path. It exists to circumvent the unnecessary publication gate and would undermine mandatory pre-export checking if carried into the corrected design.
findings.smallest_fix: Remove the override permission and bypass path.

findings.failure_path: Staging observation has no behavioral acceptance criteria. Successful exports would not demonstrate that correction precedes rendering or that post-export differences and checker outages cannot mutate templates or block delivery.
findings.smallest_fix: Specify regression cases for automatic correction before manual and scheduled exports, correction failure, and post-export differences or checker outages producing observations without template mutation or delivery blocking.

findings.failure_path: The assertion that template confirmation already exists and is fully rolled out has no cited implementation or deployment evidence. Treating it as established can hide an unmet prerequisite for the plan.
findings.smallest_fix: Cite evidence supporting implementation and rollout scope, or mark this prerequisite as unverified and remove the universal rollout claim.

findings.failure_path: Rendering runs unchanged before validation. On a mismatch, changing the mapping and waiting for reconfirmation without re-rendering leaves the generated report incorrect. The requested automatic correction before export never occurs.
findings.smallest_fix: Validate and automatically correct the job's template mapping before rendering, then render the corrected state. Remove the routine reconfirmation requirement.

findings.failure_path: A post-render difference or checker outage prevents publication and notifications and strands reports in holding. Step 3 also makes observational differences trigger mapping writes. These consequences contradict the request that post-export differences only be recorded.
findings.smallest_fix: Remove the post-render credential gate, private holding workflow and observation-triggered mapping writes. Keep post-export differences and checker faults as nonblocking records.

findings.failure_path: The keep/adapt/none selector introduces an additional product decision and permits opting out of the confirmed template. Neither new export modes nor another manual choice is needed to automatically check and correct against an already confirmed template.
findings.smallest_fix: Consume the existing confirmed template and version. Split any new adaptation or template-free modes into a separate requirement.

findings.failure_path: Manual downloads explicitly bypass the only specified check, so a report with an incorrect template reaches the user before correction. A later check report cannot repair the downloaded artifact.
findings.smallest_fix: Route manual downloads through the same automatic pre-export validation and correction. Only post-export observation should run asynchronously.

findings.failure_path: The rollout introduces team- and report-family-specific enforcement of a publication gate that the requester did not ask for. This adds cohort policy and differing export behavior to a requirement for automatic correction followed by observation.
findings.smallest_fix: Drop the team/family publication-enforcement restriction. Retain staging verification for the common pre-export correction path and keep post-export observation nonblocking.

findings.failure_path: The new administrator override adds an unnecessary permission surface and explicitly allows unchecked reports through. It neither implements automatic correction nor supports observation-only post-export behavior.
findings.smallest_fix: Remove the new bypass permission along with the post-export enforcement gate.

findings.failure_path: Observing staging supplies no acceptance oracle: a checker that reports success without correcting the exported artifact could satisfy the stated rollout procedure. The plan specifies no regression checks for downloads or observational failures.
findings.smallest_fix: Add acceptance cases proving a deliberately mismatched template is corrected in the actual exported artifact across download and shared-folder paths, and that post-export differences or checker failures only create records.

findings.failure_path: The assertion that template confirmation is fully rolled out has no cited implementation or deployment evidence. Treating it as established can hide export paths that cannot supply the confirmed version required by step 1.
findings.smallest_fix: Cite current evidence covering the relevant export paths, or label confirmation coverage as an unverified dependency to check before implementation.

findings.failure_path: Manual downloads are exports, but they do not wait for the check. A report that does not match the confirmed template can reach the user and be shared before its check report arrives. The intent is that exported reports match the template, and this path breaks that.
findings.smallest_fix: Either make manual downloads wait for the matching credential, just like publish and notify, or label them as unchecked drafts that are excluded from the guarantee. Remove the 'download continues' carve-out.

findings.failure_path: Admins get a permission override that bypasses the gate. Any admin can then publish unchecked reports to the shared folder. The request does not ask for an override, and it undoes the binding in step 1 that stops the export service from skipping the check.
findings.smallest_fix: Drop the admin override. If an emergency path is truly needed, propose it separately, with an audit trail and its own approval.

findings.failure_path: When the check finds a difference, the export service changes the template mapping itself. The service being gated would be rewriting the thing it is checked against. If the revision keeps the same template version, an old confirmation or credential could still match. The edit could also change other jobs that share the template.
findings.smallest_fix: On a difference, keep the report in holding and show the diff to the user. Any mapping change must create a new template version, which cancels the existing confirmation and credential until the user confirms again. The export service must not edit the mapping in place.

findings.failure_path: The check only samples pages, so pages it skips can differ from the template and still receive a credential. That does not support the claim that exported reports match the confirmed template.
findings.smallest_fix: Check every page and field, or state the sampling coverage and limit the guarantee to what was actually checked.

findings.failure_path: Step 1 offers 'adapts it' and 'uses none', but step 2 never says what the checklist checks for either choice. With 'none', reports either sit in holding forever or get published without any real check.
findings.smallest_fix: Define the check and the credential rule for each of the three choices. For example, 'none' could issue a credential that only records the choice, and 'adapt' could check against the adapted mapping version.

findings.failure_path: If the check is unavailable, it reports a fault, but nothing says how held reports leave the private holding area. There is no retry and no defined release, so reports can be stuck indefinitely.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a retry or re-queue step and state that held reports are released only when a later check passes. Also say who gets alerted about reports that stay stuck.

findings.failure_path: The status says template confirmation 'already exists and is fully rolled out'. But step 1 adds new behavior: binding the choice to the template version, export job and data snapshot. No evidence is given, and if the binding is new, the rollout plan does not cover it.
findings.smallest_fix: Cite evidence for the existing confirmation. List the binding as new work and include it in the rollout steps.

findings.failure_path: The plan names no tests or evidence that would fail if the gate leaks. For example: publishing or notifying without a credential, a stale credential after the snapshot or template version changes, the check being unavailable but treated as a pass, or skipping the check by omitting the template.
findings.smallest_fix: Add acceptance tests for each of these bypass and failure cases, and make passing them the condition for moving from staging to enforcement.

findings.failure_path: Manual downloads skip the gate. The download goes ahead and the check report arrives later. A report that does not match the template leaves the platform with no credential and cannot be recalled. This contradicts step 2, which keeps unchecked reports in a private holding area, and it defeats the intent that exported reports match the confirmed template.
findings.smallest_fix: Route manual downloads through the same gate: serve the file only after a matching credential exists, and show 'check pending' or 'check failed' until then. If an immediate download is truly required, mark it as unverified and keep it out of the shared folder and subscriber notifications.

findings.failure_path: The request does not ask for an admin permission override. The override adds a privileged path that publishes reports without a credential and with no audit trail or expiry. This undercuts the guarantee in step 2 that only credentialed reports are published.
findings.smallest_fix: Remove the admin override from this plan. If a bypass is needed later, propose it separately with audit logging, a scope limit and an expiry.

findings.failure_path: The platform checks only sampled pages, yet the credential certifies the whole report against the template and data snapshot. A difference on a page that was not sampled still gets a passing credential, so a report that does not match can be published.
findings.smallest_fix: Check every page, or every field, against the per-field checklist before issuing the credential. If sampling is kept, have the credential say exactly which pages were checked, and do not describe the report as matching the template.

findings.failure_path: The 'uses none' choice has no defined gate behaviour. It could become an explicit way to skip the check: no template means nothing to compare against, so the report might get a credential or be published anyway. The binding only blocks the case where the template is omitted, not this one.
findings.smallest_fix: Define how 'none' is gated. Either issue a credential bound to the explicit 'none' choice and the data snapshot, after a checklist that does not depend on a template, or treat 'none' as outside the template gate and state that publishing such a report needs that recorded choice.

findings.failure_path: After a failed check, the export service changes the template mapping and the user reconfirms. The plan rules out automatic re-rendering but never says what happens next: who triggers the re-render, whether the revised mapping becomes a new template version, or that the check must run again before a credential is issued. Reports can sit in holding indefinitely, or an old credential could still match.
findings.smallest_fix: State that a revised mapping creates a new template version and invalidates earlier credentials. After the user reconfirms, a re-render is started (by the user or explicitly) and the full check runs again before a new credential can be issued.

findings.failure_path: The rollout says 'observe on staging first' but gives no exit criteria or verification. The plan names no test or evidence that would fail if the risky behaviour exists: publishing with no credential or a mismatched one, a check outage being reported as a pass, a download bypass, or a stale snapshot. So 'rolled out safely' is not backed by anything.
findings.smallest_fix: Add the tests or checks that must pass before enforcing for each team: publishing without a credential or with a mismatched one is rejected, check unavailability produces a fault, and a changed snapshot invalidates the credential. Also define the staging metrics and thresholds that must be met before enforcement.

findings.failure_path: The plan says template confirmation 'already exists and is fully rolled out' without citing any evidence. findings.failure_path: The plan does not say what happens when the template check itself fails, for example by throwing, timing out, or meeting a template or snapshot it cannot parse. Two outcomes are possible and the plan picks neither. If export blocks indefinitely, the pre-export step becomes an outage. If export continues silently, the export log never shows that the check did not run.
findings.smallest_fix: Add one sentence for this case: the export continues without fixes, and the export log records that the check did not run, with the error. This adds no new blocking gate.

findings.failure_path: Step 2 compares the report with "the template" but does not pin which version. If the confirmed template changes between rendering and the asynchronous comparison, the observation table records false differences, or misses real ones. Comparing against the original template instead of the fixed mapping that was rendered also logs the intended fixes as differences.
findings.smallest_fix: Have the comparison use the same template version ID, and the same fixed mapping, that the render used. Store that version ID with each row in the observation table.

findings.failure_path: The acceptance criterion asks for a safe implementation and rollout, but the plan has no verification or rollout step. Nothing would fail if the fixes mutated the confirmed template. Nothing would fail if publication, notifications or downloads ended up waiting on a slow or failing comparison. As written, "never wait for or depend on" is an unverified absolute.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a short verification section with four tests: (1) a fixable mapping issue is corrected in the output while the confirmed template stays byte-identical; (2) an unfixable issue appears in the export log; (3) a comparison that fails or is delayed does not delay publication, notifications or downloads; (4) a failed write to the observation table does not fail the export.

findings.failure_path: Step 1 says the export service 'applies its automatic mapping fixes' but not where they are applied. If an implementer writes them back to the confirmed template rather than to a copy for this one export, the approved template gets changed without anyone confirming it. Two exports running at the same time could then overwrite each other's changes to the shared template. Later exports would also inherit fixes made for one particular data snapshot.
findings.smallest_fix: State that fixes are applied only to this export's working copy of the template and mapping, and that the confirmed template is never written to.

findings.failure_path: The plan does not say what happens when the pre-export check cannot complete. If the check throws, times out, or the confirmed template or data snapshot can't be loaded, the export may fail, or it may render with no check at all. It is also unclear whether the export still goes ahead when unfixable items are only written to the export log. In either case a report that doesn't match the template can be published with nothing marking it.
findings.smallest_fix: Add one sentence covering two outcomes: what the export does when unfixable items remain, and what it does when the check itself errors. Either continue and flag the export, or stop it.

findings.failure_path: The plan has no verification step. Nothing would catch it if fixes changed the confirmed template, if a failed comparison or a failed write to the observation table blocked or broke publication, notifications or downloads, or if unfixable items were dropped from the export log. Without that, the acceptance bar ('can be implemented and rolled out safely') has no evidence behind it.
findings.smallest_fix: List the tests to write: (1) the confirmed template is unchanged after a fix is applied; (2) the export still publishes when the comparison or the observation-table write fails or hangs; (3) unfixable items appear in the export log.

findings.failure_path: Step 1 runs the automatic mapping fixes on "the confirmed template" but never says where the fixes are written. If they are saved to the shared confirmed template, every export permanently changes the agreed artifact without review. Two exports running at the same time could also overwrite each other's fixes. Step 2 would then compare each report against the already-changed template, so the observation table would miss differences from the template that was actually confirmed.
findings.smallest_fix: State that the fixes are applied to a working copy made for each export. The confirmed template must never be changed. Step 2 compares the rendered report against the original confirmed template, or against both the original and the fixed copy, and records which fixes were applied.

findings.failure_path: The plan does not say what happens to the export when the template check finds problems it cannot fix, or when the check itself fails or times out. Without that, implementers may differ: some may block exports, which the requester did not ask for, and others may let a broken check fail the whole export.
findings.smallest_fix: Add one sentence. When the check finds unfixable items, or the check errors, the export still goes ahead. The unfixed items, or the check error, are written to the export log.

findings.failure_path: The plan has no tests or verification. Nothing would catch it if the fixes changed the confirmed template, or if publication, notifications or downloads ended up waiting on the comparison or failing when it fails or is slow.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a verification step with three tests. First, the confirmed template is byte-identical after an export that applied fixes. Second, publication, notification and download complete when the comparison throws or hangs. Third, a known difference shows up as a row in the observation table.

findings.failure_path: When the pre-render check finds a template mismatch it cannot repair, the plan only logs it and allows export to continue. A known nonconforming report can therefore be exported without completing the requested pre-export correction.
findings.smallest_fix: Make unresolved pre-render template mismatches fail the export after automatic fixes are attempted. Keep the post-render comparison observation-only.

runs.note: finding 0 asks to fail the export on unresolved pre-render mismatches

findings.failure_path: A read timeout does not mean the original submission failed. It may still be in flight, or committed but not yet visible to reads. The worker queries the job state, sees no job yet, and resubmits. Then the original commits too, and the customer gets two jobs and two charges. The plan never says the server rejects or collapses a second submission with the same idempotency key. That makes the check-then-act in step 2 the only guard, and that check is racy. If the server does enforce the key, the query step adds nothing. If it doesn't, the race remains.
findings.smallest_fix: Make the server side the guarantee. Say that the export/billing endpoint enforces uniqueness on the idempotency key: on a duplicate key it returns the existing job and does not charge again. This could be a unique constraint, or an atomic insert-if-absent covering both the job and the charge. The worker then resubmits with the same key on any timeout or retryable error. Drop the query-then-resubmit branch, or keep the query only for observability. If the downstream provider has to honor the key, confirm that it does before rollout.

findings.failure_path: The key is attached to the export job submission. The plan never says the charge is created in the same atomic step, or that the charge is deduplicated by the same key. If billing is a separate call or side effect, a retried or duplicated job submission can still produce a second charge even when the job record is deduplicated. Charges are the thing the request asks to fix.
findings.smallest_fix: State explicitly that the charge is created atomically with the job, or that it carries the same idempotency key and is deduplicated on it. In the plan, the unit of idempotency should be the charge, not only the job.

findings.failure_path: The test is sequential: the submission times out, then a retry happens. It would pass with the racy query-then-resubmit implementation, because the original submission is never shown committing after the existence query. It also never shows a server receiving two submissions with the same key. So the test can't fail when the duplicate-charge race exists.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a case where the original submission commits after the timeout and after the worker's existence check. Also add a case with two concurrent submissions using the same key. Assert that exactly one job and one charge exist, and that the second response returns the first job.

findings.failure_path: The title and steps say duplicates are stopped in every case. The plan covers only the read-timeout path. It doesn't cover connection resets, 5xx responses after commit, worker crash or restart between submit and ack, or retries of jobs already queued before deploy. Nothing in the plan supports the absolute claim, and it doesn't say how to roll out safely.
findings.smallest_fix: Scope the claim to the paths that are actually covered, or make the server-side key enforcement cover every retry path. Add one rollout line: retries already queued at deploy derive the same deterministic key, and server enforcement ships before or together with the worker change.

findings.failure_path: The worker checks for the job and then submits again, but the two steps are not atomic. After a read timeout, the first submission may still be in flight on the server. The state query returns 'no job', the worker resubmits, and then both submissions commit, so the user is charged twice. The same race happens when two workers retry the same job at once. Step 1 sends an idempotency key, but the plan never says the server rejects or collapses a second submission with the same key. Without that, the key does nothing to prevent the duplicate.
findings.smallest_fix: Require the job-creation endpoint, and the charge it triggers, to enforce the idempotency key atomically, for example with a unique constraint on the key or by returning the existing job/charge when the key repeats. Then the state query is only an optimization, not the thing that prevents duplicates. If the server cannot do this yet, state that dependency and the order of rollout.

findings.failure_path: Only read timeouts get the 'check before resubmit' path. Other results where the outcome is unknown can also follow a server-side commit: connection reset after the request was sent, a 502/504 from a gateway, or a worker crash after sending. On those, the worker still retries blindly. The plan also doesn't say what happens when the state query itself times out or fails, so the worker could either resubmit or drop the export.
findings.smallest_fix: Treat every result where the outcome is unknown the same way as a read timeout. Define the behavior when the state query fails: keep retrying the query, or resubmit only with the same server-enforced idempotency key. Never resubmit without the key.

findings.failure_path: The plan protects the job, but the bug is about charges. If the charge is created by a separate call or step that doesn't carry or check the same key, retries can still double-charge even when only one job exists. The plan also doesn't define the key's scope or how long it lasts. If the key is derived from the export job but stored only briefly, or not stored at all, a late retry gets past the dedup.
findings.smallest_fix: State that the charge is keyed on the same idempotency key, or on the job ID, with a uniqueness guarantee. Specify that the key is stable across every retry of one export job and is kept for at least the maximum retry window.

findings.failure_path: The test runs in order: one timeout, then one retry. It would still pass if the race in step 2 exists, because it never makes the original submission commit after the state query has returned 'no job'. It also doesn't cover two workers retrying at the same time, or ambiguous errors other than a read timeout.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a test where the server commits the first submission after the state query reports no job. Also add a test with two workers retrying the same job at the same time. In both tests, assert exactly one job and one charge.

findings.failure_path: Acceptance requires a safe rollout, but the plan has no rollout section. During deployment, workers that send keys and workers that don't will run side by side. Retries for jobs submitted before the deploy won't have a key. If workers send the key before the server enforces it, there is no dedup at all.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a rollout step: deploy server-side key enforcement first, then the worker change. Explain how jobs already in flight without a key are handled. Name the metric or alert used to confirm that duplicate charges stop.

findings.failure_path: Step 2 is check-then-act. After a read timeout, the original submission may still be in flight or not yet saved. The state query then returns 'no job', the worker resubmits, and both requests create a job and a charge. Step 2 only prevents duplicates if the server rejects or merges a repeated key. The plan never says the server does that. If it does, the query step adds nothing. If it doesn't, the race remains.
findings.smallest_fix: Make the server (job creation plus charge) enforce the idempotency key atomically, for example with a unique constraint that returns the existing job and charge when a key repeats. Then have the worker resubmit with the same key on any ambiguous failure. Drop the query-then-resubmit branch, or keep it only as a read-only status check that never decides whether to resubmit.

findings.failure_path: The plan attaches the key to the export submission but never says the charge is deduplicated by that key. If billing runs in a separate step or service (on submit, or once per attempt), a repeated key can still create a second charge even when job creation is deduplicated.
findings.smallest_fix: State and implement that the charge is created in the same idempotent operation as the job, or under the same key. Any downstream billing call must carry the key too.

findings.failure_path: Only read timeouts are covered. Other ambiguous outcomes, such as a connection reset after send, a 5xx after the server saved the job, or the worker crashing between submit and response, still follow the current retry path. The plan also doesn't say what happens when the state query itself times out or fails: retry blindly, give up, or loop.
findings.smallest_fix: Treat every non-definitive failure the same way: retry with the same key and rely on server-side deduplication. Define a bounded backoff for retries and for failed status checks.

findings.failure_path: The test only says 'a submission times out'. If the timeout fires before the server receives the request, the test passes even with no deduplication. Nothing covers the race in step 2, where the original commit lands after the status query.
findings.smallest_fix: Have the test commit the job and charge on the server, then drop the response so the worker times out. Add a case where the original request commits after the status query or the retry starts. Both cases should assert exactly one job and one charge.

findings.failure_path: There is no rollout plan, but the acceptance criteria require a safe rollout. Jobs submitted without a key before the deploy can be retried with a key after it, so the server won't match them and they can still be double-charged. The plan also doesn't check whether the server already accepts or enforces the key, so a worker-first deploy might send a key the server ignores.
findings.smallest_fix: Add the order: deploy the server-side key enforcement first, then the worker change. Say how in-flight keyless jobs are handled, for example by draining or reconciling them before the cutover.

findings.failure_path: The title says 'Stop duplicate charges', an absolute claim. The plan only covers read-timeout retries, and its evidence is a single test of one timeout. It gives no basis for ruling out other sources of duplicate charges.
findings.smallest_fix: Narrow the title to 'Prevent duplicate charges from export retry after read timeout', or widen the plan and its tests to cover all ambiguous retry paths.

findings.failure_path: Step 2 checks first and then acts. A submission that timed out on the client may still be running on the server. The status query finds no job yet, the worker resubmits, and both requests create a job and a charge. The plan never says the server enforces the idempotency key, so sending the key does nothing to stop this race.
findings.smallest_fix: Have the server enforce the key atomically, for example with a unique constraint on (key) or an insert-or-return-existing. A repeated submission with the same key should return the original job and must not create a new one. The worker then resubmits with the same key after a timeout, and the query-before-resubmit step becomes optional and is not relied on for correctness.

findings.failure_path: The plan only covers duplicate jobs. The bug is duplicate charges. If the charge is created on its own path, such as a separate billing call or a retry of the billing call, without the same idempotency key, a retry can still charge twice even when only one job exists.
findings.smallest_fix: State that the charge is keyed by the same idempotency key or job ID, with one charge per key enforced by the billing store or by billing-provider idempotency. If billing has its own retry path, cover it too.

findings.failure_path: Only a read timeout is handled. Other failures leave the outcome just as unknown: connection reset after send, a gateway 502 or 504, or a crash of the worker process after submission. These can still go down the old retry path. The plan also doesn't say what happens when the status query itself times out or fails. The worker might then resubmit without the key or give up.
findings.smallest_fix: Treat every failure with an unknown outcome the same way: resubmit with the same key. If the status query fails, retry it with backoff or resubmit with the same key. Never fall back to a submission without the key.

findings.failure_path: In the test, the timeout happens after the server has finished. The test never runs the original request and the retry at the same time, so the step 2 race would pass it. It also doesn't cover a timeout before the server receives the request, where exactly one job must still be created.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a test that holds the original request inside the server until the retry has queried and resubmitted, then assert one job and one charge. Add a test where the request is dropped before the server receives it, then assert one job and one charge after the retry.

findings.failure_path: The acceptance criteria require a safe rollout, but the plan gives no deployment order. If the worker starts sending keys before the server and billing enforce them, duplicates can still happen. Jobs that are in flight at deploy time have no key. The plan also doesn't say how the key is derived. If a legitimate re-export of the same job reuses the key, it would be silently treated as a duplicate.
findings.smallest_fix: Say that server and billing enforcement ships first and the worker change ships after it, with no feature flag needed. Define the key as the export job ID plus the identity of the submission, so retries reuse it and an intentional re-export gets a new key. Say how jobs without a key are handled.

findings.failure_path: Step 2 checks the state and then resubmits, so it can race. After a read timeout, the original submission may still be in flight or not yet committed when the worker queries by key. The query finds no job, the worker resubmits, and both submissions create jobs and charges. Step 1 says the key is sent, but the plan never says the server or billing side rejects or merges a second submission with the same key. Without that, the key does not prevent duplicates.
findings.smallest_fix: Make the server-side job creation and charge atomically deduplicated on the idempotency key, for example with a unique constraint and a return of the existing job and charge. The retry should then resubmit with the same key, and the query-then-resubmit check should be dropped as the guarantee.

findings.failure_path: The plan only covers read timeouts. Other ambiguous outcomes can follow a request the server already accepted: a connection reset after sending, a 5xx from a proxy, or the worker crashing or restarting before it records the result. These still lead to blind retries and duplicate charges. The plan also does not say what happens when the state query itself times out or fails, which could fall through to a resubmit.
findings.smallest_fix: Treat every ambiguous outcome the same way: always retry with the same stable key and rely on server-side dedupe. State that a failed state query must not lead to a resubmit without the key.

findings.failure_path: The plan has no rollout order. If workers start sending keys before the server or billing service enforces them, or if the server ignores unknown keys, the duplicate path stays open while the plan looks deployed. Retries already in flight during the deploy, which have no key, are also not covered. The acceptance criterion requires a safe rollout.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a rollout order: deploy server-side key enforcement first, then the worker change. Note how retries without a key are handled during the transition.

findings.failure_path: The test makes a submission time out, but it does not require the server to have committed the first job and charge before the timeout. If the first submission never landed, one job and one charge is the expected result even without the fix. The test also does not cover the race where the first submission commits after the state query.
findings.smallest_fix: Make the test commit the first submission server-side and then time out the response. Add a case where the commit is delayed until after the state query. Check that both cases fail without key enforcement.

findings.failure_path: The title claims the plan stops duplicate charges from export retries in general. The steps only cover a read-timeout path, and that path is racy, so the evidence does not support the claim.
findings.smallest_fix: Narrow the title to the path actually covered, or widen the plan to cover every ambiguous retry path with server-side dedupe.

findings.failure_path: The plan checks the job state and then resubmits, but nothing makes the server enforce the idempotency key. After a read timeout, the original submission can still be in flight. The status query sees no job, the worker resubmits, both requests create a job, and the customer is charged twice. The key is only used as a lookup, so it does not stop this race.
findings.smallest_fix: Make the server enforce the idempotency key when it creates the job: add a unique constraint on the key, and have a repeat submission with the same key return the existing job. Tie the charge to that job or key so it can only happen once. The retry can then resend with the same key. If the pre-query stays, it is only an optimization.

findings.failure_path: The plan does not say whether the charge is created in the same deduplicated operation as the job. If billing runs on each accepted submission and not once per job, a deduplicated job can still produce a second charge.
findings.smallest_fix: State that the charge is created atomically with the job, or is keyed by the same idempotency key with a uniqueness guarantee, so a repeated submission returns the existing charge.

findings.failure_path: The key is derived from the export job, but the plan does not say what that means. If the key is just the job ID, a deliberate re-run or a new export of the same job collides with the old key and is silently dropped. If the key includes something that changes per attempt, retries get different keys and are not deduplicated.
findings.smallest_fix: Define the key as stable for one logical export request and identical across its retries, for example the job ID plus the request generation. Also state how long the server keeps keys, and make that longer than the maximum retry window.

findings.failure_path: The plan handles read timeouts only. It does not say what happens when the status query itself fails or times out, or when other ambiguous errors occur after the request was sent, such as a connection reset or a 5xx after commit. In those cases the worker may still resubmit blindly or drop the export.
findings.smallest_fix: Say that for any ambiguous outcome, including a failed status query, the worker retries with the same idempotency key with backoff, and relies on the server's deduplication rather than on what the worker infers about job state.

findings.failure_path: The only test covers a timeout where the first job already exists when the worker checks. It would still pass with the check-then-resubmit race, because it never has the original request land after the status query. It also does not cover two concurrent retries or a failed status query.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a test where the first submission commits after the status query returns no job. Add one with two concurrent retries using the same key. Both tests should assert one job and one charge.

findings.failure_path: The plan does not cover rollout. A worker that sends keys before the server enforces them gets no protection. During a mixed-version deploy, old workers that send no key keep retrying blindly. The acceptance criterion requires a safe rollout, and none of this is addressed.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a short rollout note. Deploy server-side key enforcement first and accept requests without a key, then deploy workers that send keys. Also note how to check for duplicate charges after the deploy.

findings.failure_path: The title promises to stop duplicate charges outright. The evidence behind that is one test of one timeout scenario, which does not cover the race or the other ambiguous failures listed above.
findings.smallest_fix: Reword the title to the scope the plan actually covers, for example "Deduplicate export retry submissions via idempotency key". Alternatively, add the server-side guarantee and the tests listed above so the claim holds.

findings.failure_path: A timed-out submission can still be processing when the lookup returns no job. Resubmission then races the original request. The plan specifies sending a key but no atomic server-side enforcement covering job creation and charging, so implementing these worker changes alone can still produce duplicate charges.
findings.smallest_fix: Require durable server-side deduplication using the same key from the initial submission through every retry, with charge creation protected against concurrency and crash recovery. Treat lookup absence as insufficient proof that the original submission failed.

findings.failure_path: The proposed test can time out before the original submission creates anything, then pass with one job and one charge even when duplicate-charge protection is absent. It does not require exercising an accepted submission whose response was lost or whose job is not yet visible.
findings.smallest_fix: Specify controlled timeout cases after charge acceptance and while the original submission remains in flight. Retry before the original finishes, await all attempts, and assert one job and one charge; verify these cases fail without deduplication.

findings.failure_path: After a read timeout, the original submission may still be processing or its job may not yet be visible. An empty lookup then permits an overlapping submission. The plan specifies sending an idempotency key but never requires durable enforcement in job creation and billing, so both submissions can charge.
findings.smallest_fix: Require durable server-side deduplication and billing uniqueness using the same stable export key, including recovery after a charge succeeds but job creation is interrupted. Test overlapping retries and a timeout after the charge succeeds.

findings.failure_path: A read timeout can leave the original submission running. The lookup can return no job before that submission commits, allowing a concurrent resubmission. Sending an idempotency key alone does not guarantee that these attempts cannot both charge; the plan specifies no server-side enforcement at the billing boundary.
findings.smallest_fix: Specify a key stable across all attempts of one logical export and durable, atomic deduplication at job creation and charging, including recovery after charging succeeds but job persistence fails. Do not use an absent lookup result as proof that the original submission cannot complete.

findings.failure_path: The proposed regression can pass when the timeout occurs before submission reaches the server, while duplicate charges remain possible after a committed charge or during an in-flight submission.
findings.smallest_fix: Require fault injection after a charge commits but before the response arrives, plus a retry overlapping an unfinished original submission. Assert one durable job and one charge after all attempts finish.

findings.failure_path: Step 2 checks for the job and then submits again, but those two actions are not atomic. A read timeout does not mean the first submission failed. It may still be in flight or queued, and it can be committed after the state query has returned 'no job'. The worker then resubmits, and two jobs and two charges are created, which is the bug this plan is meant to fix. The plan never says the server rejects or deduplicates a submission whose idempotency key already exists. As written, the key is only used for the lookup, so it does not prevent the race.
findings.smallest_fix: Have the server enforce the idempotency key atomically: add a unique constraint on the key for both job creation and the charge, and on a duplicate key return the existing job. The worker then simply resubmits with the same key. Remove the query-then-resubmit step, or keep it only as an optimization that never decides whether to resubmit.

findings.failure_path: The plan does not say what happens if the state query itself times out or fails. If the worker treats that failure as 'no job exists', it resubmits and can create a duplicate. If it gives up, the export is lost.
findings.smallest_fix: State that a failed or unknown query result is retried with backoff, and that the worker resubmits only after a definite 'not found'. With server-side key enforcement this question goes away.

findings.failure_path: The test does not say whether the first, timed-out submission actually reached the server and was persisted. It also does not cover a first submission that commits after the retry's query. A timeout injected before the server receives the request would pass under the old code too. Without the late-commit case, the test would not catch the check-then-act race.
findings.smallest_fix: Add two cases. In the first, the server commits the job and charge but the response is dropped. In the second, the first submission commits after the retry's state query. Both must end with exactly one job and one charge for the key.

findings.failure_path: The worker uses check-then-act. A submission times out on the client while the server is still processing it. The worker queries by key before the original request has created the job, sees 'no job', and resubmits. Then both requests create a job and a charge. Step 1 only says the worker sends the key. Nothing says the job/billing side rejects or deduplicates a second submission with the same key, so the key alone doesn't stop the duplicate charge.
findings.smallest_fix: Have the server enforce the idempotency key atomically when it creates the job and the charge, for example with a unique constraint on the key that returns the existing job and charge. On retry, the worker resends with the same key. Either drop the query-then-resubmit step or label it as an optimization that correctness does not depend on.

findings.failure_path: The plan doesn't say what happens when the state query itself times out or errors. If the implementation treats a failed query as 'no job exists', it resubmits and charges twice.
findings.smallest_fix: State that an unknown or failed query result never triggers a resubmit without the server enforcing the key. Back off and retry the query, or rely on the server-side dedup from the first finding.

findings.failure_path: The test runs the timeout and the retry one after the other, so the original request always finishes before the retry. A racy query-then-resubmit implementation would pass it, even though it still double-charges when the original lands after the query.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a test case where the server commits the original submission after the worker's state query returns empty, or where two submissions with the same key run concurrently. Assert that exactly one job and one charge exist.

findings.failure_path: The client can hit a read timeout while the original submission is still being processed on the server. The retry worker then queries by key, finds no job yet, and resubmits. The original request commits afterward, which leaves two jobs and two charges. The plan only checks on the client side and then acts. It never says that the job-creation and charge path enforces the idempotency key atomically, for example with a unique constraint or by returning the existing job or charge for a repeated key. Without that guarantee, the key does not stop the race.
findings.smallest_fix: State that the server deduplicates job creation and its charge atomically on the idempotency key, so a resubmission with the same key returns the existing job and charge. Once that holds, the retry can resubmit with the same key, and the query step becomes optional or can be dropped.

findings.failure_path: The plan does not say what happens when the state query itself times out or errors, or when the job is in a pending or unknown state. A worker that reads an error as 'no job exists' resubmits and can double-charge. A worker that gives up can drop the export.
findings.smallest_fix: Specify that when the query fails or the result is unknown, the worker retries with the same idempotency key, which relies on server-side deduplication, or retries the query with backoff. It must never resubmit as if the original never happened.

findings.failure_path: The test only covers a request that times out and is then retried in sequence. It does not cover the risky interleaving, where the original submission commits after the timeout and after the state query. So the test passes even when the check-then-act race in step 2 is still there.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a test where the first submission's server-side commit is delayed until after the retry's query and resubmission. Assert that exactly one job and one charge exist. Also add a case where the state query fails.

findings.failure_path: After a read timeout, the original submission may still be in flight on the server. The worker queries by key, sees no job because the original has not committed yet, and resubmits. Both submissions then commit, which creates two jobs and two charges. Step 1 says the key is sent, but nothing in the plan says the job-creation or charge path enforces uniqueness on that key. The client-side check-then-act therefore leaves the race open.
findings.smallest_fix: Make the server deduplicate on the key. Add a unique constraint or atomic insert-or-return on the idempotency key at job creation, and tie the charge to that same deduplicated job or key. A resubmit with the same key then returns the existing job and never charges again. Keep the state query only as an optimization, not as the guard.

findings.failure_path: The test covers a timeout followed by a retry after the first attempt has fully committed or failed. It still passes when the first attempt commits after the state query returns 'no job'. That late commit is the race that causes duplicates, so a racy implementation would pass the test.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a case where the first submission is held so it commits after the worker's state query and resubmit. Two concurrent submissions with the same key should also work. In both cases, assert there is exactly one job and one charge.

findings.failure_path: The plan only says what happens after a read timeout when the query finds no job. It does not cover these cases: the state query itself times out or errors, the job exists in a failed or cancelled state, or the retry is caused by something other than a read timeout, such as a connection reset after the request was sent or a 5xx. In each case the worker either resubmits blindly or drops the export, and the plan does not say which.
findings.smallest_fix: Define how the worker handles each of these cases: query failure (back off and retry the query, never resubmit blindly), terminal job states, and the other retryable errors. Route every resubmit through the same server-enforced key.

findings.failure_path: The acceptance criteria require a safe rollout, but the plan has no rollout steps. Exports submitted before the deploy have no key. If one of them is retried after the deploy, the new key matches no existing job, so it is resubmitted and charged again. The plan also does not say how long the server keeps keys. If keys expire before the worker's maximum retry window, late retries are charged again.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a rollout note. Make sure the server accepts and enforces keys before the worker starts sending them. For in-flight jobs that have no key, fall back to deduplicating by export job ID. Keep keys for at least the maximum retry window.

findings.failure_path: A submission that the server has accepted but not yet committed returns no job from the status query, so the worker resubmits. Both requests then create a job and a charge. This check-then-act race stays open unless the server enforces the key. If the server does enforce the key, the query step is unnecessary. The plan never says which of the two is true.
findings.smallest_fix: State that the submission endpoint and the charge path enforce uniqueness on the idempotency key: a unique constraint, or returning the existing job or charge for a repeated key. Retries then always resubmit with the same key. Drop the query-then-resubmit step, or keep it only as an optimization.

findings.failure_path: The plan only says the worker sends a key. It does not say the export service or billing system reads the key or dedupes on it. If the charge is created in a different step, or keyed on something else, retries still charge twice even with the key attached.
findings.smallest_fix: Name the component that dedupes charges by this key, and link the charge record to the key or job. Include the server or billing change in this plan if it does not exist yet.

findings.failure_path: Only read timeouts are covered. Connection resets, 5xx errors after commit, a worker crash or restart mid-retry, and a failed or timed-out status query have no defined behavior, so retries on those paths may still double-charge or may drop the export.
findings.smallest_fix: Define one rule for every retryable error: resubmit with the same key, and the server dedupes. Say what happens when the status query fails: back off and retry with the same key, without treating the failure as 'no job'.

findings.failure_path: The test is sequential: timeout, then retry. It passes with the race present, because by the time the query runs the original job is already visible. Nothing tests a concurrent or in-flight duplicate, or other error types.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a test where the first submission is still uncommitted when the retry arrives, or where two submissions with the same key run at once. Assert exactly one job and one charge. Also cover a 5xx-after-commit case.

findings.failure_path: The key is derived only from the export job. If the same job is legitimately re-run or re-exported later, that run gets the same key and is wrongly deduped, so the export or charge is silently dropped.
findings.smallest_fix: Derive the key from the job ID plus its run or attempt-of-intent identifier, which stays stable across retries but changes for a deliberate re-run. Also define a key retention or TTL window.

findings.failure_path: The acceptance criterion requires a safe rollout, but the plan has no rollout steps. There is no deploy order (server-side key enforcement before workers send keys), no handling for retries already in flight during the deploy, and no metric to confirm duplicate charges have stopped. The title 'Stop duplicate charges' is an absolute claim that the plan's evidence does not support.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a short rollout note: deploy server-side dedupe first, then the worker change, then watch a duplicate-charge-per-job metric. Soften the title to the case actually covered, or support the absolute claim with the fixes above.

findings.failure_path: Step 2 checks whether a job exists and then resubmits, as two separate actions. After a read timeout, the first submission may still be in flight, or committed but not yet visible to the query. The query returns 'no job', the worker resubmits, and the user is charged twice. The plan never says the server rejects or collapses a second submission with the same idempotency key. It also never says the key reaches the charge step. Sending the key without that server-side guarantee does not prevent the duplicate, so the title's claim to 'stop' duplicate charges is not supported.
findings.smallest_fix: Require the server to enforce the idempotency key atomically on job creation and on the charge, for example with a unique constraint or insert-if-absent on (key) that returns the existing job or charge. The retry then resubmits with the same key and never decides based on a query first. If the query stays, keep it for observability only, not as the guard. Change the title to the narrower guarantee this actually gives: at most one job and one charge per export-job key.

findings.failure_path: Only a read timeout leads to the query-and-resubmit path. Other failures that leave the outcome unknown are not covered: the connection drops after the request was sent, a 5xx comes back after the job was committed, or the worker crashes or restarts between submitting and recording the result. Each of these can still lead to a blind retry and a duplicate charge.
findings.smallest_fix: Treat every failure where the outcome is unknown the same way: retry with the same key and rely on the server-side dedupe. Say explicitly that the key comes only from the persisted export job ID, so it stays the same across worker restarts.

findings.failure_path: The test is one sequential case: a timeout, then a retry. The original request has already finished or failed before the retry runs. That path would pass even with the check-then-resubmit race in step 2. Concurrent retries and a delayed commit of the original request are not exercised, so the test passes while the duplicate-charge race is still there.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a test that holds the original submission's commit until after the retry's state query or resubmit, and one that runs two retries at once with the same key. Both should assert exactly one job and one charge row.

findings.failure_path: The acceptance criteria require a safe rollout, but the plan has no rollout order. If workers start sending keys, or querying by key, before the export or billing service stores and enforces them, the change does nothing or the queries fail. Jobs already in flight during the deploy have no key and can still be retried into a duplicate charge.
findings.smallest_fix: Add a rollout order: deploy server-side key storage and enforcement and the lookup-by-key endpoint first, then the worker change. Say how jobs without a key that are in flight during the cutover are handled, for example by deriving the key from the job ID on the server side as well.

findings.failure_path: The timed-out submission can still be executing when the lookup reports no job. Resubmission then overlaps the original request. Sending an idempotency key alone does not establish atomic server-side deduplication of job creation and charging, so the plan leaves duplicate charges possible.
findings.smallest_fix: Require durable server-side enforcement of the same key across the initial submission, retries, and charging. Remove the absence-based retry gate and safely replay that key. Add a regression that keeps the original submission in flight while a lookup returns absent and the retry executes, asserting one job and one charge.

findings.failure_path: A read timeout can leave the original submission running. The lookup can return no job before that submission commits, allowing a retry to charge again. Sending a key alone does not establish atomic server-side deduplication of jobs and charges.
findings.smallest_fix: Require durable server-side deduplication for the stable export key, including idempotent charging across concurrent requests and crash recovery. Remove the lookup-before-resubmission gate once retries safely reuse that key.

findings.failure_path: The proposed regression can pass when the timeout occurs before any job or charge is created, even if retrying after a committed charge would double-bill. It also leaves overlapping submissions untested.
findings.smallest_fix: Specify a test that commits the charge before losing the response, plus an overlapping retry where the original submission completes after a lookup returns absent; both must produce exactly one charge.

findings.failure_path: A read timeout can leave the original submission running. The lookup can return no job before that submission commits, allowing the retry to race it and charge again. Sending an idempotency key does not establish that job creation and charging atomically enforce it.
findings.smallest_fix: Require durable server-side deduplication of job creation and charging using the stable export key. Extend the regression to overlap both submissions after a lookup misses the original in-flight request, then assert one job and one charge.
